subtype: Approach: deciding purpose and audience first [Thinking]
passage:
“Before you press share, tell me one thing,” Vidya Masi said. “Why are you posting it?”
Mahima looked at her sketch of the monsoon terrace. “I want people to see it.”
“Which people?”
“Not everyone.” She frowned. “Amma, Nani, my friends from class. Not strangers who say weird things about my drawings.”
“So who should be able to see it?”
“Only people I know. Which means a private account, not a public one.” She flipped the settings on her phone, laughing as she switched on approval for followers. “And I only post art. No location, no school uniform, no midnight selfies.”
“Sounds like a plan.”
“It's my plan. I made it.”

qa.q: Who does Mahima want to see her art?
qa.a: Mahima wants Amma, Nani and her friends from class to see it.

qa.q: What does Mahima's reply, It's my plan, I made it, suggest she feels?
qa.a: Mahima feels proud and independent, since she worked out the purpose and the rules herself.

qa.q: What could Mahima do if a stranger asks to follow?
qa.a: She could decline or ignore the request and keep the account private, since her purpose is to share with people she knows.

qa.q: How might Nani see Mahima's private account?
qa.a: Nani may feel happy and included, since she is one of the chosen viewers and can enjoy the art safely.

grounding: A teen asks why she is posting, chooses to share art with friends and family only and makes the account private so purpose shapes what goes up.

subtype: Approach: thinking before posting with a simple test [Thinking]
passage:
Wednesday, 10:30 pm.
Typed a long angry post about how Sharmila's half of our group project came in a day late again. It felt AMAZING to type. Thumb over Post. Then I remembered my own test: would I be fine if Mrs Kapoor, Papa and someone hiring me ten years from now all read this? Teacher: no. Papa: definitely not, he'd ask why I didn't just talk to her. Future boss: probably decides I'm someone who trashes teammates. I deleted the draft and texted Sharmila instead: “Can we put dates next to each task?” Amma says her boy has a temper. Tonight the temper stayed in my notes app, and nobody saw the ugly version. Test passed. I'm using it again.
— Rehan

qa.q: Who does Rehan imagine reading his post?
qa.a: Rehan imagines Mrs Kapoor, Papa and someone hiring him ten years from now.

qa.q: What was Rehan feeling when he typed the angry post?
qa.a: Rehan was angry, and venting felt amazing, until his own test made him uneasy.

qa.q: What else could Rehan try about the late work?
qa.a: Rehan could talk to Sharmila and, if needed, the teacher about clear dates, which he began by texting about dates for each task.

qa.q: How might Sharmila see the text about dates?
qa.a: Sharmila may find it reasonable and much less hurtful than a public rant, so she can fix the delay without being shamed.

grounding: A student asks whether a teacher, a parent and a future employer would be fine with the post and keeps an angry rant off the internet.

subtype: Approach: audit of privacy settings and old posts [Action]
passage: Bidisha, I'll tell you what I did last Sunday, because it took only an hour. I'm Mridula, the sensible girl in our lane according to the aunties, and my cousin, who works in tech and says she reviews hers monthly, told me to look at my account the way a stranger would. So I did. First, tags: three photos where friends had tagged me with our club's full name. I asked them to remove it. Then location: I switched it off in every app, because my posts basically told anyone when I'm at tuition. Then I scrolled far down to a photo from Class Eight: me in uniform at the school gate, the name board behind me. I deleted it. Anyone could work out where I'll be at eight in the morning. Nothing scary has happened. But now nothing about my routine is public.

qa.q: What did Mridula delete?
qa.a: Mridula deleted a photo from Class Eight of her in uniform at the school gate with the name board behind her.

qa.q: Why did Mridula switch off location?
qa.a: She was worried that her posts told anyone when she was at tuition, so strangers could work out her routine.

qa.q: What else could Mridula do to protect her account?
qa.a: She could check who follows her, keep the account private and repeat the review every few months, since old posts pile up.

qa.q: How might Mridula's friends feel when asked to remove tags?
qa.a: They may feel surprised at first, but most would understand since Mridula explains it is about privacy, not about them.

grounding: A teen reviews tags, location sharing and public photos, removes an old post showing the school gate and uniform and switches off location.

subtype: Approach: setting time boundaries for use [Action]
passage:
Study hall in the hostel started at seven, and Yash slid his phone into his locker with the notifications already switched off. Shankar, at the next desk, raised an eyebrow. “No reels tonight?”
“Two windows a day,” Yash said. “Half past six for twenty minutes, and nine o'clock for twenty minutes. That's it. I posted my match photo at 6:40 and read the replies. Now I'm done.”
“And exam weeks?”
“Only the evening window. Sometimes not even that.”
“I check mine about forty times an hour,” Shankar muttered.
“That's why I set the windows. The phone follows my rules now.”
Yash opened his chemistry notes. Shankar stared at his own pocket and did not take the phone out.

qa.q: When are Yash's two windows for using his phone?
qa.a: The windows are half past six and nine o'clock, twenty minutes each.

qa.q: What might Shankar be feeling as he stares at his own pocket?
qa.a: Shankar may feel tempted and a little envious, and perhaps uneasy about how often he checks.

qa.q: What could Shankar try for himself?
qa.a: Shankar could start with one window and turn off notifications, then adjust, since a rule he sets works better than willpower alone.

qa.q: How might friends who message Yash at other times feel?
qa.a: They may be a little annoyed at slow replies, but once they know about the windows they can expect an answer at those times.

grounding: A student limits posting and checking to two windows a day, turns off notifications and stays nearly offline in exam weeks.

passage:
During chemistry, Dorje checked his phone under the desk again: 212 likes yesterday, 148 now. His stomach dropped. Madhuri leaned over from the next bench. “You look like you failed a test.”
“Likes are down. I need something bolder.” He had already posted the neon-dyed hair photo, then a pouting close-up he didn't even like, and each time the number jumped, he felt light for an hour. Then it dipped, and he felt heavy again. All day his mood moved with a counter he couldn't control. At lunch he opened the app twelve times. Madhuri said quietly, “You were happier when you posted the picture of your dog.” Dorje shrugged, but he put the phone face down for the rest of the lesson.

qa.q: How many likes did Dorje's post have yesterday, and how many now?
qa.a: It had 212 likes yesterday and 148 now.

qa.q: How is Dorje feeling as the likes drop?
qa.a: Dorje feels anxious and heavy, since his stomach dropped and his mood moves with the counter.

qa.q: What could Dorje try instead of chasing bolder pictures?
qa.a: Dorje could post what he enjoys, like the picture of his dog, and check less often, since his mood should not depend on numbers he cannot control.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see Dorje's chasing of likes?
qa.a: Madhuri seems concerned but gentle, since Madhuri remembers when Dorje looked happier and says so quietly.

grounding: A teen posts bolder pictures to gain followers, feels anxious when likes drop and finds his mood tied to numbers he does not control.

subtype: Approach: comparing with edited lives of others [Pitfall]
passage: The power had gone off in the evening, and Ayesha lay under the quilt scrolling by her phone's light. A girl from her old school in the city stood on a white beach in a yellow dress. Another post: three friends at a rooftop café, glowing. Ayesha looked at her own day: helping at the family's stationery counter, an argument on the school bus, dal for dinner. It all seemed grey, and her chest sank. Next morning at the school gate she told Lalremsiami, “Everyone's life is better than mine.” Lalremsiami laughed. “You know they took thirty tries for that beach photo, right? Nobody posts the bus argument.” That night Ayesha unfollowed nine accounts that always left her low, and kept the ones that made her laugh or learn.

qa.q: What was Ayesha doing at the family's stationery counter?
qa.a: She was helping at the family's stationery counter.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling as she scrolled under the quilt?
qa.a: Ayesha felt low and dissatisfied, since her chest sank as she compared her grey day with the glowing photos.

qa.q: What could Ayesha remember or try when this mood returns?
qa.a: She could remind herself that posts are chosen highlights and keep trimming what she follows, or talk with friends about real days.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami see the polished photos?
qa.a: Lalremsiami sees them as staged, and laughs gently while pointing out that the beach photo took thirty tries.

grounding: A student sees polished holiday photos and feels her own life is lacking, forgetting posts are chosen highlights, until she trims whom she follows.

passage:
“Mummy, can I show you something? Don't be angry.” Manoj held out his phone.
Minakshi read the message slowly. It said: Which school do you go to? Send your number and house area.
“Who is this?”
“I don't know. I accepted them last month. I wanted more followers.” His voice cracked. “They keep messaging. I didn't reply. Should I?”
“No. Thank you for showing me.” She took a breath and put an arm around his shoulders. “Let's block the account and report it together, right now.”
“Am I in trouble?”
“No. You did the right thing by coming to me. And tomorrow we'll go through who follows you and remove anyone you don't know.”
Manoj tapped Block, and his shoulders dropped an inch.

qa.q: What did the stranger's message ask for?
qa.a: The message asked which school Manoj goes to and for his number and house area.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when he showed his mother the phone?
qa.a: Manoj was nervous and afraid of being in trouble, since his voice cracked as he asked whether he should reply.

qa.q: What could Manoj do from now on?
qa.a: Manoj could accept only people he knows, review his followers with a parent and keep the account private.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel about her son coming to her?
qa.a: Minakshi is probably worried but also relieved and proud that Manoj told her, since she stays calm and thanks him.

grounding: A teen accepts follows from unknown accounts to look popular, later gets a private message pressing for personal details and tells a parent and blocks the account.

subtype: Approach: handling a negative comment by pausing [Revision]
passage: The comment said my drawing looked like a kindergarten project, from an account with a blank profile picture. My face went hot and my fingers were already typing something nasty. I'm Tushar, and I want to tell you what I did instead: I put the phone in the other room for one hour. I ate a banana and walked around the block. After the hour, the reply I'd wanted to write sounded silly, even to me. So I ignored it, deleted the comment and blocked the account. Then I texted Rukmini, who calls me bhai: “Someone was mean online, feeling weird.” She sent back, “Want to call?” We talked for ten minutes. No argument, no audience, and by dinner my drawing looked fine again.

qa.q: How long did Tushar wait before deciding what to do?
qa.a: Tushar put the phone in the other room for one hour.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he read the comment?
qa.a: Tushar felt hurt and angry, since his face went hot and he started typing something nasty.

qa.q: What could Tushar do if the comments keep coming?
qa.a: Tushar could report the account and tell a trusted adult, since repeated meanness is not something to handle alone.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel on receiving the text?
qa.a: Rukmini probably feels concerned and glad that Tushar reached out, since she answers at once and offers a call.

grounding: After a mean comment, a teen waits an hour, decides to ignore it, deletes and blocks, and later checks in with a friend instead of arguing.

subtype: Approach: using it for a real interest and learning [Action]
passage:
Dear Jagdish Mama,
You asked how I use my phone these days, since you worried it was all reels. Here's the update. I unfollowed the meme pages and now follow three science teachers and two coding channels, one of which explains electronics with just a battery and a bulb. Last month I asked our robotics sir, Mr Pillai, whether I could make a page for the club. He said yes, as long as he checks each post before it goes up, and no faces of younger kids without permission slips. The page has 62 followers so far, including a girl from another school who is building a line-follower like ours and sent me a sensor idea. I've learned more this month than in two months of scrolling. Thanks for pushing me.
Your nephew, Tanay

qa.q: What condition did Mr Pillai set for the club page?
qa.a: Mr Pillai said he checks each post before it goes up, and no faces of younger kids without permission slips.

qa.q: How does Tanay feel about the change, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Tanay feels proud and energised, since he says he learned more this month than in two months of scrolling.

qa.q: What could Tanay do to keep the connections safe?
qa.a: Tanay could keep sharing only club work, keep the teacher approving posts and keep messages from strangers to public comments.

qa.q: How might Jagdish Mama feel reading the email?
qa.a: Jagdish Mama is probably relieved and pleased, since the worry that it was all reels has turned into real learning.

grounding: A student follows science teachers and coding channels, makes a robotics club page with a teacher's approval and finds connections that support his goals.

passage: The hostel allowed phones for one hour after dinner, and Pema had already spent forty minutes on his anger. Sonali had told the whole class about his failed audition. In the last twenty minutes he typed: “Some people can't keep a secret to save their lives.” Post. Two minutes later the phone went into the warden's box. All night the sentence sat in his head. In the morning at 6:50, in the queue for the phone, he deleted the post first, then wrote to Sonali: “That post was about you, and it was unkind. I was angry about the audition. I'm sorry.” She replied at lunch: “Thanks. I shouldn't have told.” On the back of his hand Pema wrote in ink: no posting when upset. Two weeks later it was still there, half smudged.

qa.q: What did Pema write on the back of his hand?
qa.a: Pema wrote in ink: no posting when upset.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when he wrote the post?
qa.a: Pema was angry and hurt about his failed audition and Sonali telling the class.

qa.q: What could Pema have done instead of posting?
qa.a: Pema could have talked to Sonali privately about the secret or written the angry words in a private note, since a post cannot easily be taken back.

qa.q: How might Sonali have felt about the post, and then the apology?
qa.a: Sonali was probably hurt and embarrassed by the post, and the apology gave her a chance to admit her own part.

grounding: After posting something unkind in anger, a teen deletes it, apologises to the person and sets a rule not to post when upset.
